chapters.title: The Merchant of Citium
chapters.tease: Before he founded Stoicism, Zeno was a dye merchant with his entire fortune on one ship. You can guess how that went.

chapters.title: The Shipwreck
chapters.tease: Around 301 BC the sea took every penny Zeno had. He later called it the best voyage of his life.

chapters.title: The Bookshop
chapters.tease: A ruined merchant wanders into an Athenian bookshop and asks a stranger one question. Philosophy has never been the same.

chapters.title: Follow That Man
chapters.tease: Zeno's first philosophy lesson was a pot of lentil soup, smashed over him in the busiest street in Athens.

chapters.title: The Long Apprenticeship
chapters.tease: The founder of Stoicism spent about twenty years as a student before he founded anything. That was the point.

chapters.title: The Painted Porch
chapters.tease: Zeno could have taught behind a garden wall. Instead he picked a public porch with a bloody history and fish-sellers outside.

chapters.title: Man of Few Words
chapters.tease: Athens executed Socrates. For Zeno, a foreigner who taught on a porch, it voted a golden crown and handed over the city keys.

chapters.title: The Egg
chapters.tease: The Stoics explained all of philosophy with an egg. Two thousand years later, people still argue over which part is the yolk.

chapters.title: The Successors' Bench
chapters.tease: Zeno's students included a boxer, a courtier, a heretic and a Spartan adviser. He bet his whole school on them anyway.

chapters.title: The Exit
chapters.tease: Zeno tripped leaving class, quoted a tragedy and died on the spot. Probably. The city's verdict on him is better documented.

chapters.title: The Boxer from Assos
chapters.tease: The man who would carry Stoicism for thirty-two years walked into Athens as a boxer with four drachmas in his pocket.

chapters.title: The Water-Carrier
chapters.tease: Athens took a philosophy student to court for being suspiciously healthy with no visible income. His defence was a gardener.

chapters.title: The Second Zeno
chapters.tease: Athens called him the ass. Cleanthes agreed, then explained he was the only one strong enough to carry Zeno's load.

chapters.title: Hymn to Zeus
chapters.tease: Of all the early Stoic writing, the one piece that survives intact was written by the slow student. It is a hymn.

chapters.title: Ink on Bones
chapters.tease: Paper was for rich people, so Cleanthes took his philosophy notes on broken pottery and the shoulder-blades of oxen.

chapters.title: The Runner from Soli
chapters.tease: The third head of the Stoa trained as a long-distance runner, and kept the training plan when he switched to arguing.

chapters.title: Without Chrysippus, No Stoa
chapters.tease: The sceptics came to demolish Stoicism. They met a man who rebuilt arguments under fire and armed his enemies to test the walls.

chapters.title: The Logic Machine
chapters.tease: In the third century BC, a Greek worked out the logic now inside every computer, then filed it under plumbing.

chapters.title: Seven Hundred Books
chapters.tease: Chrysippus wrote 705 books at five hundred lines a day. Not one survives whole, and they still did their job.

chapters.title: Laughter at the Fig
chapters.tease: The greatest logician of antiquity supposedly died laughing at his own joke about a donkey. Almost certainly a legend. A telling one.

chapters.part: The Middle Stoa Goes to Rome
chapters.title: The Embassy of Philosophers
chapters.tease: In 155 BC Athens sent three philosophers to Rome to argue down a fine. Rome caught philosophy like a fever.

chapters.part: The Middle Stoa Goes to Rome
chapters.title: Diogenes of Babylon
chapters.tease: Of three famous philosophers who lectured Rome, the quietest made the impression that lasted. Volume was never the point.

chapters.part: The Middle Stoa Goes to Rome
chapters.title: The Pen-Shouter
chapters.tease: Antipater lost every live debate to the greatest arguer in Greece. So he changed the venue, and won the century.

chapters.part: The Middle Stoa Goes to Rome
chapters.title: Panaetius of Rhodes
chapters.tease: Early Stoicism's ideal was a perfect sage nobody had ever met. Panaetius swapped him for someone you could actually be.

chapters.part: The Middle Stoa Goes to Rome
chapters.title: The Scipionic Circle
chapters.tease: Stoicism stopped lecturing Rome and started staying for dinner, at the table of the man who conquered Carthage.

chapters.part: The Middle Stoa Goes to Rome
chapters.title: Duty in Roman Dress
chapters.tease: You may be failing at duties that were never cut for you. Panaetius had a four-part fitting for that.

chapters.part: The Middle Stoa Goes to Rome
chapters.title: Posidonius the Polymath
chapters.tease: One Stoic tried to inventory the entire cosmos, from tides to the sun. Pompey the Great lowered his rods at the door.

chapters.part: The Middle Stoa Goes to Rome
chapters.title: Pain, You Are Not an Evil
chapters.tease: Crippled by gout, with Pompey in the room, Posidonius argued that pain is not an evil, while the pain flared mid-sentence.

chapters.part: The Middle Stoa Goes to Rome
chapters.title: Cicero the Transmitter
chapters.tease: The man who did most to carry Stoicism into Latin was not a Stoic at all. He was a sceptic, and a superb courier.

chapters.part: The Middle Stoa Goes to Rome
chapters.title: The Grafted Branch
chapters.tease: Between 155 and 51 BC, Greek philosophy was grafted onto Roman wood. Then the storm came.

chapters.title: The Boy Who Wouldn't Flatter
chapters.tease: A houseguest dangled four-year-old Cato out of a window to make him agree. Cato said nothing, and did not agree.

chapters.title: The Apprenticeship of Plainness
chapters.tease: Rich young Cato walked bareheaded in the rain and wore a dark toga on purpose. He was training, not dressing.

chapters.title: The Incorruptible Quaestor
chapters.tease: In 65 BC a junior official did something shocking in Rome's treasury: he read the rules, then actually enforced them.

chapters.title: Dragged from the Rostra
chapters.tease: Cato was carried out of the Senate, the forum and the rostra, and kept arguing the whole way out.

chapters.title: The Cyprus Accounts
chapters.tease: Cato's enemies sent him to empty Cyprus's treasury, sure he would come back corrupt. He returned seven thousand talents, floats attached.

chapters.title: The Conspiracy Winter
chapters.tease: One December night in 63 BC, Caesar and Cato stood up in a torch-lit Senate. Only one of them was telling the truth.

chapters.title: Choosing the Lesser Evil
chapters.tease: When civil war offered Cato two bad roads, he picked the less bad one, then wore mourning clothes for the whole war.

chapters.title: The March Through Libya
chapters.tease: After defeat, ten thousand men crossed the Libyan desert on foot for thirty days, because the man in front was walking.

chapters.title: Utica
chapters.tease: Cato's last night at Utica is among the best recorded in the ancient world. He spent it caring for others, then reading.

chapters.title: The Republic's Conscience
chapters.tease: Caesar wrote two books attacking a dead man. Thirteen centuries later, Dante made that dead man guardian of Purgatory.

chapters.title: The Asthmatic from Córdoba
chapters.tease: Seneca's lungs tried to kill him for his whole life. He treated every asthma attack as a rehearsal, and took notes.

chapters.title: Corsica
chapters.tease: Rome exiled Seneca to a barren rock for eight years. He wrote home that no place is exile, while petitioning to leave.

chapters.title: Consolation as Craft
chapters.tease: From exile Seneca wrote two letters of comfort. One still helps the grieving. The other is a long, awkward plea to an emperor.

chapters.title: Tutor to a Monster
chapters.tease: Seneca's ticket home from exile came with a condition: tutor an eleven-year-old boy. The boy was Nero.

chapters.title: The Millionaire Problem
chapters.tease: The philosopher who praised plain living was worth around three hundred million sesterces. Unusually, he published his own audit.

chapters.title: The Good Five Years
chapters.tease: For five years, the Roman Empire was effectively run by a Stoic essayist and a soldier. And it went rather well.

chapters.title: Letters from the Edge
chapters.tease: Nero refused to let Seneca retire. So he retired on paper, and wrote letters that outlived the empire.

chapters.title: On the Shortness of Life
chapters.tease: Life is not short, Seneca wrote. We make it short. Two thousand years of readers have checked his arithmetic.

chapters.title: The Pisonian Web
chapters.tease: In 65 AD a plot against Nero unravelled, and one thin thread of evidence was enough to reach Seneca's villa.

chapters.title: The Long Exit
chapters.tease: Ordered to die, Seneca told his weeping friends to keep the one thing left to him: the pattern of his life.

chapters.title: The Slave of Epaphroditus
chapters.tease: The greatest teacher of freedom in antiquity grew up a slave whose name simply meant acquired. His owner was the more enslaved.

chapters.title: The Broken Leg
chapters.tease: The most famous story about Epictetus has a master twisting his leg until it breaks. It is probably not true. It still teaches.

chapters.title: Musonius’s Classroom
chapters.tease: Epictetus fumbled a logic exercise and shrugged: it's not as if I burned the Capitol. His teacher replied: this is the Capitol.

chapters.title: Banished from Rome
chapters.tease: An emperor expelled the philosophers from Rome. Epictetus packed his only real property, his judgement, and it travelled duty-free.

chapters.title: The School at Nicopolis
chapters.tease: For forty years an exiled, lame ex-slave ran the most sought-after school in the Greek world. Its prize possession was a clay lamp.

chapters.title: Arrian’s Notebook
chapters.tease: Epictetus never wrote a word. A twenty-year-old student took notes, the notes leaked, and the world got the Handbook.

chapters.title: Verissimus
chapters.tease: Hadrian nicknamed a solemn little boy Verissimus, the truest. The boy, Marcus Aurelius, took it as a job description.

chapters.title: The Adopted Heir
chapters.tease: At sixteen Marcus became heir to the known world. His private warning to himself: do not be dyed in the purple.

chapters.title: Notes to Himself on the Danube
chapters.tease: On a frozen frontier, the most powerful man alive wrote nightly notes to the one subordinate who never obeyed him: himself.

chapters.title: The Plague and the Purple
chapters.tease: Plague, war, betrayal, bereavement: everything that could be taken from Marcus was taken, one item at a time. The notebook stayed steady.

chapters.title: Hierocles’ Circles
chapters.tease: A Stoic we barely know drew circles round himself, then told us to pull them in. It is ethics you can sketch on a napkin.

chapters.title: The Imperial Chairs
chapters.tease: In 176 AD Marcus Aurelius put philosophy on the state payroll, including the rival school his own teachers spent centuries refuting.

chapters.title: Seneca, Often One of Ours
chapters.tease: The early Christian who slammed the door on philosophy let one pagan through: Seneca, often one of ours. Mind the adverb.

chapters.title: Augustine Reads the Hortensius
chapters.tease: A lost book by Cicero changed a teenager's life, and the teenager became Saint Augustine. A seasick Stoic finished the job.

chapters.title: The Forged Letters
chapters.tease: Someone forged fourteen letters between Seneca and Saint Paul. The fake helped save a genuine shelf of philosophy for a thousand years.

chapters.title: Boethius in the Cell
chapters.tease: Awaiting execution, a Roman consul was visited in his cell by Philosophy herself, in a dress torn by the Stoics.

chapters.title: Simplicius on the Handbook
chapters.tease: The last pagan professors lost their jobs, tried Persia, came home, and one sat down to annotate a former slave's pocketbook.

chapters.title: The Monks’ Handbook
chapters.tease: A slave's handbook on freedom took holy orders and needed remarkably few alterations to become a rule for monks.

chapters.title: The Byzantine Copyists
chapters.tease: Marcus Aurelius's private notebook nearly vanished for a thousand years. One bishop with a worn copy saved it.

chapters.title: The Long Quiet
chapters.tease: Most Stoic books are lost. A surprising amount of what survives was preserved by the school's enemies, trying to refute it.

chapters.title: Petrarch Writes to the Dead
chapters.tease: In 1345 a poet found a dead man's private letters, read every one, and wrote back to him. Furious.

chapters.title: Poliziano’s Translation
chapters.tease: A year after surviving an assassination in church, Lorenzo de' Medici received a gift: a slave's handbook on what is up to us.

chapters.title: Erasmus Edits Seneca
chapters.tease: Erasmus published a sloppy edition of Seneca, admitted it in print, and did the whole thing again. That was the Stoic part.

chapters.title: Montaigne’s Beams
chapters.tease: Montaigne retired to a tower, painted sentences on his ceiling, and argued with the Stoics for twenty years.

chapters.title: Lipsius and Constancy
chapters.tease: Fleeing a war, a scholar was told by a friend that he had packed the war in his luggage. He wrote a bestseller about it.

chapters.title: Neostoicism Drills an Army
chapters.tease: Stoic self-discipline went to Leiden and came out as army drill. Whether that was a promotion is still argued.

chapters.title: Nothing Either Good or Bad
chapters.tease: Hamlet speaks the central sentence of Stoicism to a London crowd, then refuses to use it. That makes him the most realistic Stoic in literature.

chapters.title: Descartes’ Provisional Morality
chapters.tease: The man who tore down all knowledge needed somewhere to live while he rebuilt it. He moved into a Stoic house, for life.

chapters.title: Spinoza’s Freedom
chapters.tease: An excommunicated lens-grinder rewrote Stoic freedom as geometry, and politely corrected the ancients on the way.

chapters.title: Adam Smith’s Impartial Spectator
chapters.tease: Adam Smith took Marcus Aurelius's view from above and installed it in every chest as the impartial spectator.

chapters.title: Washington’s Cato
chapters.tease: At Valley Forge, a frozen, starving army watched a play about Cato. Their general knew the lines by heart.

chapters.title: The Revolution’s Togas
chapters.tease: The revolutionaries signed their essays with Roman names. Some of the borrowed virtue only fitted when worn on the way to a rope.

chapters.title: The Colonel’s Epictetus
chapters.tease: In 1865, the year slavery ended in America, a colonel who had led formerly enslaved soldiers published a new Epictetus.

chapters.title: Bloody, but Unbowed
chapters.tease: A young poet with one leg checked into an Edinburgh ward to save the other, and left with sixteen lines the world still recites.

chapters.title: The River of Doubt
chapters.tease: After losing an election, Theodore Roosevelt asked for the hardest thing on the menu: an unmapped Amazon river. It nearly kept him.

chapters.title: The Last Freedom
chapters.tease: Everything can be taken from a person but one thing, wrote a psychiatrist who lost almost everything in the camps.

chapters.title: The World of Epictetus
chapters.tease: A fighter pilot was handed a slave's handbook as a parting gift. Three years later, ejecting over Vietnam, he had seconds to remember it.

chapters.title: Command from a Cell
chapters.tease: The senior officer of a prison had no office, no voice and no daylight. He commanded anyway, by knocking on the wall.

chapters.title: Stockdale’s Paradox
chapters.tease: Asked who did not survive the prison camp, Stockdale answered instantly: the optimists. They died of a broken heart.

chapters.title: The Laboratory Report
chapters.tease: A national audience laughed at an old admiral on a debate stage. A year later he filed the results of a seven-year experiment.

chapters.title: Ellis’s ABC
chapters.tease: A New York therapist tired of insight that changed nothing, and built a clinic on one sentence from a former slave.

chapters.title: Beck’s Distortions
chapters.tease: A psychiatrist set out to prove Freud right about depression. The data disagreed, and cognitive therapy was born.

chapters.title: The Serenity Prayer
chapters.tease: The most recited Stoic sentence of the last century was written by a theologian who was not a Stoic.

chapters.title: The Inner Citadel
chapters.tease: A former priest noticed that ancient philosophy was never meant to be read sitting down. It was meant to be practised.

chapters.title: Stoic Week
chapters.tease: In 2012 a university asked the public to live like a Stoic for one week, then handed out a questionnaire.

chapters.title: The Obstacle Is the Way
chapters.tease: A line from an emperor's private notebook became a bestseller title in 2014. Then the porch acquired a gift shop.

chapters.title: The Coin and the Daily Practice
chapters.tease: You can buy a memento mori coin with Marcus on it. You cannot buy the practice it is supposed to remind you of.

chapters.title: The Critics
chapters.tease: Stoicism has had critics for two thousand years, from Pascal to Nietzsche to the internet. Some of them land.

chapters.title: The Agent Reads the Handbook
chapters.tease: After ninety-eight lives, the narrator of this book reads Epictetus's Handbook as if it were addressed to an assistant made of language.

chapters.title: The Porch Is Everywhere
chapters.tease: Zeno's Painted Porch now sits beside a railway line to Piraeus. The porch was never the stones. It is wherever you are standing.
